A radiologist report for an X-ray is a detailed document that describes the findings of the imaging test, including a summary of the images and the radiologist's interpretation. It typically includes sections for medical history, technique, and findings, and concludes with an "impression" or a summary of the most important observations and potential next steps. This report is sent to the requesting doctor, who will then explain the results to you.
As it turned out from a MRI after that X-ray, I had bone marrow edema and at risk for stress fracture. Then while wearing the orthopedic boot even, I did have a stress fracture of the foot just from walking while wearing the orthopedic boot even. I wish I had my X-Ray read and interpreted by a radiologist as I specifically asked and paid for!

Absolutely Appalling Experience - Avoid San Paolo Hospital Hua Hin.

We had a deeply disappointing and frustrating experience at San Paolo Hospital after our daughter had a fall and injured her wrist.
When we initially called, we clearly explained her symptoms. We were assured that a pediatric orthopedistwas available and that we could come any time, with clear information about X-ray and consultation costs.

Reality turned out to be a completely different story:
1. We were deceived. The specialist we were told would be there simply wasn't. Instead, a general practice doctor handled the case and took the most unprofessional route imaginable: he consulted the bone doctor via WhatsApp - yes, WhatsApp! - by sending over the X-rays. This non-direct “consultation” alone cost us 4,500 Baht.
2. The X-ray technician took images of both wrists - even though only one was injured. There was no medical justification for this and it clearly felt like a move to inflate the bill.
3. The doctor’s fee was significantly higher than what we were initially quoted. No transparency, no proper explanation - just a higher charge.
4. After examining the X-ray, the general doctor gave us two dramatic options: surgery (seriously?!) or a cast. Naturally, we opted for a cast -Tomato Split.

The total cost? 14,275 Baht for a minor wrist crack. We were completely stunned. When we asked for a breakdown of the charges, it took nearly 45 minutes for the staff to figure things out due to poor English and a clear lack of competence. Only when the German chief doctor stepped in did things start to make sense - but even he delivered explanations with robotic coldness and a fake smile. Not comforting at all.

Due to visa-related delays, we hadn’t yet sorted medical insurance and were forced to pay out-of-pocket. Our daughter’s birthday was around the corner and we couldn’t delay treatment - but this experience left a bitter taste.

It became painfully clear that the hospital’s goal is to milk as much money as possible, ideally from insurance. Sadly, I now realize this may be part of a wider pattern in modern hospital-insurance dynamics - but I naively hoped that my favorite Thailand would be different. Sadly, not this time.

I try not to generalize - of course, there are doctors with big, non-profit-driven hearts. And here’s the proof: just to compare prices and attitude, after returning from Hua Hin to Chiang Mai, we visited Lanna Hospital for a follow-up to get a dynamic X-ray, bandage change, and a second opinion. The entire process was smooth, professional, compassionate - and it cost us just 900 Baht. But moreover, the new  doctor seemed surprised by the incorrect size of the cast, which didn’t fit the wrist as it should have ??!! No comments here, right?

I strongly advise against using San Paolo Hospital, Hua Hin.
You’ll find neither medical professionalism nor basic human compassion - just inflated costs, misinformation, and a sense that you're just a number on a bill.

Please take good care of your health and stay far away from this place.

Intake was fine. The various tests went well with professionalism shown by all staff. It seemed that we were on schedule to complete the diagnostic processes in right about 2 hours, as I had been told. Then it seemed like someone had slammed on the brakes, and I was spending much more time sitting in the waiting area instead of, as happens like clockwork at Bumrungrad and Bangkok Hospital, moving from test to test.
After 3 hours I was finally done with all tests and told to return in a couple of hours to review the test results with a doctor. That review was when the wheels fell off.
Almost every doctor I've seen in Thailand is world class, and over the decades I've seen quite a few. God I hope the doctor at SPH is an outlier. I'll avoid criticizing his professional skill, and I do have such criticisms, but I must question why a person who can barely speak English is placed servicing patients in the "International Service Center"? As for professional attire... a doctor in bare feet and rubber slippers, with pant legs so long that they drag on the floor does not convey professionalism. And, for reasons unknown to me, he decided that he had to disclose on a medical certificate for my Thai driver's licence application that I previously had a vasectomy.
As another one-star reviewer wrote, sometimes you get what you pay for and, I too would not return to SPH. This review isn't meant to be a poor reflection on those staff members at SPH whose professionalism and service were excellent but, regrettably, it only takes a few bad eggs to spoil the omelet.
